A heuristic evaluation is `a usability inspection method where UX specialists check a computer interface against established rules of thumb (heuristics) to find design problems`.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heuristic_evaluation)[[2]](https://fuselabcreative.com/heuristic-evaluation-in-ux-usability-guide/)

### Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics

The most common framework is **Jakob Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics** , which guides how interfaces should behave:[[1]](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)[[2]](https://fuselabcreative.com/heuristic-evaluation-in-ux-usability-guide/)

- **Visibility of System Status:** The system should always keep users informed about what is happening through clear feedback.
- **Match Between System and Real World:** The system should use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user rather than internal jargon.
- **User Control and Freedom:** Users often make mistakes and need a clear "emergency exit" (like undo or redo) to leave unwanted states.
- **Consistency and Standards:** Follow platform and industry conventions so users do not have to wonder whether different words or actions mean the same thing.
- **Error Prevention:** A careful design that prevents a problem from occurring is even better than a good error message.
- **Recognition Rather than Recall:** Minimize the user's memory load by making objects, actions, and options visible.
- **Flexibility and Efficiency of Use:** Accelerators—hidden from novice users—may speed up the interaction for the expert user.
- **Aesthetic and Minimalist Design:** Dialogues should not contain irrelevant or rarely needed information.
- **Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors:** Error messages should be expressed in plain language, precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
- **Help and Documentation:** Even though it is better if the system can be used without documentation, it should be easy to search and focus on the user's task.[[1]](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)


---

### How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation
The process is structured to be fast and cost-effective:[[1]](https://fuselabcreative.com/heuristic-evaluation-in-ux-usability-guide/)

1. **Assemble Evaluators:** Use 3 to 5 independent UX specialists or designers rather than just one person (a single evaluator typically catches only about 35% of problems).
2. **Set the Scope:** Define the specific user flows, screens, or features to inspect.
3. **Independent Inspection:** Each evaluator goes through the interface alone over 1 to 2 hours, first to learn the system and second to log heuristic violations.
4. **Rate and Consolidate:** The team meets to merge lists, rate issues by severity and business impact, and eliminate false positives.
5. **Produce Recommendations:** Turn the findings into a prioritized action plan for the design team.[[1]](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-to-conduct-a-heuristic-evaluation/)[[2]](https://fuselabcreative.com/heuristic-evaluation-in-ux-usability-guide/)[[3]](https://ixdf.org/literature/topics/heuristic-evaluation)


---

### Benefits and Limitations

- **Pros:** Fast, inexpensive, easy to run early in the design cycle, and highlights major structural flaws before you spend money on full user testing.
- **Cons:** It relies on the skill of the evaluators, can generate false alarms, and does **not** replace real-world user testing.[[1]](https://ixdf.org/literature/topics/heuristic-evaluation)[[2]](https://maze.co/guides/usability-testing/heuristic-evaluation/)[[3]](https://fuselabcreative.com/heuristic-evaluation-in-ux-usability-guide/)[[4]](https://thedecisionlab.com/reference-guide/design/heuristic-evaluation)
